A general tensor-structured compression scheme for efficient large language models

Ying Lu Affiliation: School of Physical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100049, China Affiliation: Kavli Institute for Theoretical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China    Peng-Fei Zhou Affiliation: Center for Quantum Physics and Intelligent Sciences, Department of Physics, Capital Normal University, Beijing, 100048, China    Qi-Xuan Fang Affiliation: School of Physical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100049, China Affiliation: Kavli Institute for Theoretical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China    Pan Zhang Affiliation: Institute of Theoretical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China    Shi-Ju Ran Email: sjran@cnu.edu.cn Affiliation: Center for Quantum Physics and Intelligent Sciences, Department of Physics, Capital Normal University, Beijing, 100048, China    Gang Su Email: sugang@itp.ac.cn Affiliation: School of Physical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100049, China Affiliation: Kavli Institute for Theoretical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China Affiliation: Institute of Theoretical Physics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China
Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) are dominated by dense linear transformations, whose storage, memory and computational overheads hinder efficient adaptation and deployment while masking the functional impacts of structural simplification. Here we present Tensor Mixture (MixT), a general tensor-structured compression scheme that replaces targeted dense linear layers with natively executable mixtures of tensor operators. Operating directly on generic linear projections instead of model-specific components, MixT is potentially applicable across Transformer-based LLMs and other dense neural mappings. We evaluate MixT on Qwen3-8B and LLaMA2-7B under a unified recovery protocol, identifying a broad compressible regime in which MMLU accuracy is largely preserved before an abrupt transition at model-specific boundaries. This transition coincides with coordinated shifts in output entropy, prediction entropy and inter-layer geometry. At the LLaMA2-7B transition boundary, MixT reduces full-model parameters by 47.5%, inference FLOPs by 37.1%, training FLOPs by 52.1% and peak inference memory by 60.4%, demonstrating its practical potential for lower-cost LLM compression.

LLMs have achieved impressive performance, but dense parameterizations drive rapid growth in storage, memory and computation [1, 2, 3]. This has motivated strong interest in efficient and structured model designs that reduce cost while preserving capability, including parameter-efficient adaptation [4], quantization [5, 6, 7, 8, 9], pruning and structural compression [10, 11, 12, 13, 14], and layer-level modification or removal [15, 16]. Recent studies suggest that tolerance to structural simplification is depth dependent: some layers or substructures can be altered with little loss, whereas others remain tightly coupled to model function [15, 16, 17, 18]. Complementary evidence from neural-language alignment studies also points to depth-organized functional hierarchy, reinforcing the view that layer roles are non-uniform across model depth [19]. However, existing approaches are usually judged by final accuracy–efficiency trade-offs [20], which offers limited insight into how performance evolves along a controlled compression path within Transformer blocks [21]. More broadly, for models dominated by dense and weakly structured parameterizations, a framework is still needed that makes structural complexity explicit and allows compression depth to be scanned in a controlled and comparable way.

In quantum many-body physics and multilinear algebra, tensor methods provide a principled way to manage the accuracy–efficiency trade-off by combining compact representations with explicit internal structure and systematic control over order, mode size and connectivity [22, 23, 24]. These properties enable efficient representations of otherwise intractable systems while retaining interpretability of how global behaviour emerges from local interactions [22, 24]. A similar challenge appears in large-scale machine learning, where dense parameterizations obscure the internal organisation of model interactions. This parallel suggests that tensor-structured representations are a natural way to inject explicit structure into neural computations.

While tensorized approaches have been explored for compression, reparameterization, embedding compression and efficient adaptation in neural networks and NLP [25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30], many tensorized parameterizations for LLMs reconstruct dense weights or do not fully preserve structured execution in the forward computation path [31]. As a result, their impact on runtime computational and memory efficiency can remain constrained, limiting the potential practical benefits of tensor-based compression techniques.

In this work, we introduce Tensor Mixture (MixT), a tensor-structured framework that replaces standard dense linear transformations in Transformer blocks with directly executable tensor operators, making structural complexity explicit and controllable (Figure 1). Figure 1 summarises the MixT construction, including block-level replacement of Transformer linear maps, NTN_{T}-controlled operator scaling and a dataset-specific empirical scaling comparison between dense Qwen3 base models and recovered MixT descendants of Qwen3-8B. MixT rewrites dense mappings as mixtures of coupled local tensor components, enabling structural complexity to be controlled along two axes: local tensor structure and replacement depth. Because MixT operates on dense linear projections rather than model-specific modules, it is potentially applicable to a broad class of Transformer-based LLMs; here we evaluate this property on two representative 7B/8B-scale model families. By retaining structured operators in the forward path, MixT provides a route to lower storage, computational cost and memory usage.

We apply MixT to progressive structural simplification in Qwen3-8B [32] and LLaMA2-7B [33], treating compression depth NBN_{B} as an explicit control variable. In both settings, the models show a broad region in which substantial structural reduction causes little performance loss, followed by an abrupt transition beyond a model-specific boundary. This transition is accompanied by coordinated shifts in output-distribution statistics and internal representations, including abrupt changes in answer entropy, prediction entropy and inter-layer geometry under prompting. These results suggest that structural simplification in the tested LLMs can exhibit critical-like behaviour: performance declines smoothly up to a threshold, and then degrades sharply. MixT therefore provides a controlled framework for locating benign simplification regimes and probing transition boundaries along the efficiency–performance trade-off.

Results

Abrupt transition boundary under progressive back-to-front MixT compression

Figure 2 shows that the tested LLMs admit substantial structural compression under MixT, while performance on Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) [34] remains nearly unchanged across a wide range of compression depths NBN_{B}. This indicates a broad regime in which a large fraction of each model can be structurally simplified with little MMLU loss. However, this stability breaks down abruptly once the transition boundary (denoted N~B\tilde{N}_{B}) is crossed. For Qwen3-8B, the abrupt transition occurs at approximately N~B≃11\tilde{N}_{B}\simeq 11, whereas for LLaMA2-7B it occurs at N~B≃17\tilde{N}_{B}\simeq 17. Beyond these boundaries, replacing only one or two additional blocks is sufficient to induce large degradation, in some cases reducing accuracy close to random-guessing level. The transition is therefore abrupt rather than gradual.

Within this sweep, the transition boundary provides the strongest structural simplification before the sharp performance drop. Taking LLaMA2-7B with the number of tensor branches NT=4N_{T}=4 as an example, a representative dense output projection is reduced from 16.7816.78M parameters to about 1.051.05M (6.25% of the original). This yields an estimated whole-model size of 3.54B parameters, corresponding to a 47.5% reduction from the 6.74B dense baseline (52.5% remaining).

The transition boundary is relatively stable within each tested model. Varying the internal complexity of the MixT operator, for example by changing the number of tensor branches (NTN_{T}), has only a minor effect on N~B\tilde{N}_{B}. Even under aggressive operator-level compression above 98% (NT=5N_{T}=5 for a single linear map), the transition threshold in Qwen3-8B remains near N~B≃11\tilde{N}_{B}\simeq 11. The performance curve nevertheless becomes more irregular, with increased variability emerging in the pre-transition regime (NB<N~BN_{B}<\tilde{N}_{B}).

The inset of Fig. 2(b) shows that compression behaviour is strongly direction dependent. When the same procedure is applied from earlier to later layers, performance deteriorates immediately and monotonically, without an extended stable regime or a comparable abrupt-transition threshold. This asymmetry indicates that tolerance to structural simplification is not uniform across depth, with earlier layers exhibiting substantially greater sensitivity, consistent with previous reports of depth-dependent functional specialization in LLMs [29, 15, 16].

Optimal resource gains

Table 1 compares LLaMA2-7B with its MixT-structured counterpart at the transition boundary. Parameter complexity is reduced by approximately a factor of two, indicating that a large fraction of the model can be structurally simplified without immediate loss of MMLU performance. This reduction is accompanied by substantial computational savings: inference cost decreases from 726.78726.78 to 457.34457.34 GFLOPs, and training cost decreases from 27.0627.06 to 12.9712.97 TFLOPs. These gains are possible because MixT keeps the tensor-structured operator in the forward path rather than reconstructing a dense weight matrix before computation. The effect is particularly pronounced for training, reflecting the compounding impact of structural simplification across the full forward–backward pipeline.

These reductions are accompanied by lower measured peak memory usage in the tested implementation. Although profiling was performed on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU, the measured peak memory of the reported MixT setting falls below 2424 GB for both inference and recovery training, suggesting potential feasibility on 2424-GB-class accelerators. The reported training configuration corresponds to optimising all parameters within the compressed MixT structure, rather than those of the original dense model.

The parameter reduction also directly lowers storage requirements under standard numerical precision. Because MixT operates at the level of structural re-parameterisation, it is complementary to numerical compression techniques such as quantisation and can be combined with them to achieve further reductions in storage. Taken together, these results show that the transition boundary marks not only an abrupt functional transition, but also a potentially useful operating regime in which substantial resource reductions can be realised before sharp MMLU degradation.

Output-distribution statistics

We next ask whether the abrupt transition reflects only a drop in benchmark accuracy or also a change in output behaviour. Figure 3 shows that both occur on MMLU. For both Qwen3-8B and LLaMA2-7B, crossing the transition boundary is accompanied by an abrupt accuracy drop and a sharp change in output-distribution statistics.

Figure 3a,b first shows a clear change in output entropy. Before N~B\tilde{N}_{B}, accuracy remains relatively stable and OE, defined in Eq. 3, stays low, indicating that the model usually concentrates probability mass on a small subset of answer options for each question. Once N~B\tilde{N}_{B} is crossed, OE rises abruptly while accuracy falls. The transition boundary therefore marks a sudden loss of per-question decisiveness, rather than a gradual weakening of performance alone.

Prediction entropy behaves differently. OE is defined from the full four-way answer distribution on each MMLU question, whereas PE, defined in Eq. 4, is computed from the distribution of final predicted labels over the full evaluation set. In both sweeps, PE is high before the boundary and drops after it. This means that the post-transition model becomes not only more uncertain on individual questions, but also more concentrated in its final label usage across the dataset.

To place these compressed checkpoints in a broader context, Fig. 3c,d compares them with a wider set of LLMs spanning different scales. Across this model set, OE decreases approximately linearly with MMLU accuracy, whereas the transformed prediction entropy, −log10⁡(1−PE)-\log_{10}(1-\mathrm{PE}), increases approximately linearly. Using MMLU accuracy as a fraction, the empirical linear trends are

OE\displaystyle\mathrm{OE} ≈1.20−1.30​Acc,\displaystyle\approx 1.20-1.30\,\mathrm{Acc},
−log10⁡(1−PE)\displaystyle-\log_{10}(1-\mathrm{PE}) ≈−0.90+4.87​Acc.\displaystyle\approx-0.90+4.87\,\mathrm{Acc}.

The MixT checkpoints follow the same broad trends traced by baseline models of different scales. The output statistics observed near the transition boundary are therefore not isolated anomalies of a single compression sweep, but part of a broader empirical relation between answer-distribution structure and task performance.

Inter-layer geometry drift aligns with the transition boundary

Figure 4 shows how inter-layer geometry changes across the compression sweep. For each checkpoint, we compare the inter-layer similarity map with that of the dense reference and measure their absolute deviation by Δ​SNB​(ℓ,ℓ′)\Delta S_{N_{B}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime}), defined in Eq. 5. Larger values indicate larger departures of the corresponding layer pair from the dense model.

To visualize how this drift evolves along the full compression path, we first average Δ​SNB​(ℓ,ℓ′)\Delta S_{N_{B}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime}) over all valid end layers ℓ′>ℓ\ell^{\prime}>\ell for each start layer ℓ\ell. This gives an all-end-layer drift profile,

Δ​S¯NB​(ℓ)=⟨Δ​SNB​(ℓ,ℓ′)⟩ℓ′>ℓ.\overline{\Delta S}_{N_{B}}(\ell)=\left\langle\Delta S_{N_{B}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime})\right\rangle_{\ell^{\prime}>\ell}.

The resulting landscape shows that geometry drift is weak at early compression depths, but becomes structured as NBN_{B} approaches the transition boundary (Figure 4a). Near N~B=17\tilde{N}_{B}=17, high-drift regions are already visible, whereas after the boundary the drift expands over a broader range of start layers. Thus, the transition boundary separates an early weak-drift regime from a post-boundary regime in which inter-layer geometry changes become more spatially extensive.

To quantify these changes, Figure 4b compares two summary statistics: mean drift over layer pairs near the output end and mean drift over all valid layer pairs. The output-side average rises with compression and reaches a high value around the transition boundary. By contrast, the global average is well described by two empirical trend bands: a pre-boundary regime with a scaling coefficient of about 0.006 per compressed block, and a post-boundary regime with a larger coefficient of about 0.016 per compressed block. These two regimes share a linear scaling form but differ in scaling coefficient. The intersection of the two empirical trend bands occurs near NB=N~BN_{B}=\tilde{N}_{B}. This indicates that the transition boundary is not only associated with strong output-side distortion, but also marks the onset of faster global geometry drift.

Discussion

We developed MixT as a tensor-structured compression framework for dense linear layers and used it to study how performance changes under progressive back-to-front structuring for LLMs. Across both Qwen3-8B and LLaMA2-7B, the same overall pattern emerges on MMLU: performance remains stable over a broad range of compression depths and then drops sharply once the number of compressed blocks NBN_{B} crosses a model-dependent transition boundary. In this sense, MixT does more than provide a compressed alternative to dense layers. It turns compression depth into an explicit structural coordinate and makes failure onset measurable along a controlled compression path.

This framework also shows practical potential. MixT yields substantial reductions in parameter count, storage footprint, training and inference complexity, and memory usage in the tested setting. These reductions are not limited to severely degraded regimes, but already appear where MMLU performance remains near the pre-transition level. MixT therefore provides a useful compromise between structural simplicity and retained capability. Equally importantly, these gains rely on retaining the structured operator directly in the execution path rather than using tensorization only as a compressed parameterization (e.g., [31]). The compression path is explicit, tunable and comparable across depths, making it possible to relate resource reduction to the point at which performance ceases to remain stable.

The abrupt transition observed during progressive MixT simplification exhibits characteristics of a critical-like transition. This shift is marked by abrupt performance degradation and coordinated alterations in output statistics and inter-layer geometry. These findings suggest that the tested models undergo functional reorganisation from a stable, well-structured regime to a sharply degraded state. This behaviour provides a controlled setting for studying how structural simplification affects functional integrity and for identifying thresholds at which simplification remains effective before severe degradation. The emphasis on executable structure rather than parameter count alone is also consistent with recent evidence that functional behaviour can be traced along constrained, approximately invariant paths in parameter space [35].

While this study demonstrates MixT’s potential efficiency and effectiveness under a fixed post-compression recovery protocol, its full potential remains to be explored in more complex real-world settings. In particular, integrating reinforcement learning and high-quality long-reasoning-chain data remains an important direction for future work, especially for tasks requiring multi-step reasoning. The present results were obtained with an early MixT implementation and a comparatively modest recovery protocol; substantial engineering work on tensor kernels, recovery data, alignment and hardware-aware execution may further improve the performance of MixT and related tensor-structured AI methods. MixT is not a replacement for existing LLM techniques such as quantization and training algorithms, but is complementary to them and may enable further resource reductions while preserving, or potentially enhancing, performance on complex tasks. This positions MixT as a promising framework for future model optimisation.

Methods

MixT architecture

MixT (Mixture of Tensors) is a structured replacement for dense linear layers, including those in Transformer models. As illustrated in Fig. 1, the replacement is applied to all linear layers in each selected Transformer block, spanning both the self-attention and feed-forward submodules. In the back-to-front compression sweep, NBN_{B} denotes the number of Transformer blocks in which all linear layers are replaced under the block-level MixT configuration.

For a linear layer ff with input and output dimensions DinD_{\mathrm{in}} and DoutD_{\mathrm{out}}, we write Din=dnD_{\mathrm{in}}=d^{n} and Dout=dmD_{\mathrm{out}}=d^{m}, where dd is the local bond dimension used for tensorization. If an input or output dimension is not exactly expressible as a power of dd, zero padding is applied before tensorization.

The input is reshaped into nn bonds of dimension dd and processed by NTN_{T} parallel branches. Each branch applies one local tensor of input order n−NT+1n-N_{T}+1 and output order m−NT+1m-N_{T}+1. After all branches are evaluated, their outputs are summed, multiplied by 1/NT1/N_{T}, and reshaped back to the output dimension of the original linear layer. Taking m=n=5m=n=5 (that is, a linear layer of dimensions 25×252^{5}\times 2^{5}) and NT=4N_{T}=4 as an example, the MixT map is expressed as

f⁡(𝒙)=∑j1​j2Ti1​i2​j1​j2[1]​xj1​j2​i3​i4​i5+∑j2​j3Ti2​i3​j2​j3[2]​xi1​j2​j3​i4​i5\displaystyle f(\boldsymbol{x})=\sum_{j_{1}j_{2}}T^{[1]}_{i_{1}i_{2}j_{1}j_{2}}x_{j_{1}j_{2}i_{3}i_{4}i_{5}}+\sum_{j_{2}j_{3}}T^{[2]}_{i_{2}i_{3}j_{2}j_{3}}x_{i_{1}j_{2}j_{3}i_{4}i_{5}}
+∑j3​j4T[3]i3​i4​j3​j4xi1​i2​j3​j4​i5+∑j4​j5T[4]i4​i5​j4​j5xi1​i2​i3​j4​j5,\displaystyle+\sum_{j_{3}j_{4}}T^{[3]}_{i_{3}i_{4}j_{3}j_{4}}x_{i_{1}i_{2}j_{3}j_{4}i_{5}}+\sum_{j_{4}j_{5}}T^{[4]}_{i_{4}i_{5}j_{4}j_{5}}x_{i_{1}i_{2}i_{3}j_{4}j_{5}},
(1)

where 𝒙\boldsymbol{x} denotes the input and {𝑻[k]}\{\boldsymbol{T}^{[k]}\} (k=1,…,NTk=1,\ldots,N_{T}) denote the weight tensors for the MixT branches. We use a bold letter (for example 𝒙\boldsymbol{x}) to denote a tensor and the same letter with indices (for example xi1​i2​i3​i4x_{i_{1}i_{2}i_{3}i_{4}}) to denote its elements. For simplicity, we fix the branch number NTN_{T} to control the compression strength of an individual linear replacement.

Scaling of parameter count and FLOPs: asymptotic exponential reduction

Consider a dense linear layer with dimensions Hout×HinH_{\mathrm{out}}\times H_{\mathrm{in}} and parameter count N=Hout​HinN=H_{\mathrm{out}}H_{\mathrm{in}}. After tensorization, we write Hin=dnH_{\mathrm{in}}=d^{n} and Hout=dmH_{\mathrm{out}}=d^{m}, so that N=dm+nN=d^{m+n}. In the square case shown in Fig. 1b, Hin=Hout=HH_{\mathrm{in}}=H_{\mathrm{out}}=H, and for the default setting d=2d=2, this gives m=n=log2⁡Hm=n=\log_{2}H. Taking NTN_{T} branches, the parameter count of each branch is Nbranch=dm+n+2−2​NTN_{\mathrm{branch}}=d^{m+n+2-2N_{T}}, and the total parameter count of a MixT satisfies N′=r​NN^{\prime}=rN with the remaining parameter ratio

r=d2​NTd2​NT=NTd2​NT−2,r=\frac{d^{2}N_{T}}{d^{2N_{T}}}=\frac{N_{T}}{d^{2N_{T}-2}}, (2)

where dd denotes the dimension of each bond in the weight tensor of MixT. This indicates an asymptotic exponential compression of the parameter count.

The same reduction is obtained for theoretical FLOPs. The FLOP scaling for each MixT branch is FB∝dm+n+2−2​NTF_{B}\propto d^{m+n+2-2N_{T}}. With NTN_{T} branches, the total MixT operator scales as F′∝NT​dm+n+2−2​NTF^{\prime}\propto N_{T}d^{m+n+2-2N_{T}}. Compared with the dense-layer scaling F∝dm+nF\propto d^{m+n}, this gives F′=r​FF^{\prime}=rF, with rr the remaining ratio given in Eq. (2).

Weight-matching initialization and post-compression recovery

After structural replacement and weight-matching initialisation, each compressed checkpoint underwent a fixed-budget post-compression recovery stage. This was done to ensure that differences across compression depth reflected structural replacement rather than unequal recovery budgets. Unless otherwise stated, all checkpoints were aligned under the same training configuration and the same recovery budget of 30003000 optimisation steps, using a fixed general instruction-tuning mixture to restore broad language-model functionality after replacing dense linear layers with MixT operators.

General reasoning performance was evaluated primarily on MMLU [34] using the Language Model Evaluation Harness [36]. For each model family and local MixT setting, we progressively increased the number of back-to-front compressed blocks NBN_{B}, constructed each checkpoint from the same dense base model, aligned it under the fixed protocol above, and measured the resulting post-alignment MMLU accuracy.

We define the block transition threshold N~B\tilde{N}_{B} as the smallest compression depth at which the MMLU trajectory leaves the pre-transition plateau and enters a sustained sharp-degradation regime. Operationally, N~B\tilde{N}_{B} was taken as the first onset of an abrupt drop after which performance did not recover to the pre-transition level at larger NBN_{B}. Unless otherwise specified, compression proceeded from the output side towards the input side. A front-to-back sweep was also evaluated for comparison.

Output entropy and prediction entropy

To characterize how answer distributions change under progressive structural compression, we analyzed the four-way answer distribution over the MMLU answer tokens A, B, C, and D. Each question was evaluated in the 5-shot next-token setting used for the MMLU experiments in this work. We restricted the final-step logits to the four answer tokens and renormalized them with a softmax. This yields, for each evaluation instance, a normalized four-way answer distribution {pj}j∈{A,B,C,D}\{p_{j}\}_{j\in\{A,B,C,D\}}, with ∑jpj=1\sum_{j}p_{j}=1.

We summarize per-question uncertainty by the normalized output entropy

OE=𝔼⁡[H4]log⁡4,H4(p)=−∑j∈{A,B,C,D}pjlogpj,\mathrm{OE}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[H_{4}]}{\log 4},\qquad H_{4}(p)=-\sum_{j\in\{A,B,C,D\}}p_{j}\log p_{j}, (3)

where the expectation is taken over evaluation instances. Low OE indicates that the model concentrates probability mass on a small subset of answer options for an individual question, whereas high OE indicates a flatter four-way answer distribution.

We summarize dataset-level answer usage by the normalized prediction entropy

PE=Hpredlog⁡4,Hpred=−∑j∈{A,B,C,D}fjlogfj,\mathrm{PE}=\frac{H_{\mathrm{pred}}}{\log 4},\qquad H_{\mathrm{pred}}=-\sum_{j\in\{A,B,C,D\}}f_{j}\log f_{j}, (4)

where y^\hat{y} denotes the final predicted answer for an evaluation instance, and fj=Pr⁡(y^=j)f_{j}=\Pr(\hat{y}=j) is the empirical frequency of final predicted labels across the full evaluation set. Thus, OE is defined on the full four-way predictive distribution for each question, whereas PE is defined on the distribution of final predicted labels over the dataset [37].

Inter-layer geometry drift

To track how layer-to-layer relations change under progressive compression, we computed inter-layer similarity maps at the answer-decision position, following the broader use of representation-similarity analyses to compare hidden-state geometries across neural networks [38, 39]. For each MMLU prompt, this position is the token immediately preceding answer-token prediction. We used the same fixed prompt set for the dense reference model and for all compressed checkpoints.

Let 𝒬\mathcal{Q} denote this prompt set, and let hℓ(NB)​(q)h^{(N_{B})}_{\ell}(q) be the hidden state at layer ℓ\ell and the answer-decision position for prompt qq in the checkpoint compressed to depth NBN_{B}. For each valid layer pair (ℓ,ℓ′)(\ell,\ell^{\prime}) with ℓ′>ℓ\ell^{\prime}>\ell, we define the inter-layer similarity map as

SNB​(ℓ,ℓ′)=1|𝒬|​∑q∈𝒬cos⁡[hℓ(NB)​(q),hℓ′(NB)​(q)].S_{N_{B}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|}\sum_{q\in\mathcal{Q}}\cos\!\left[h^{(N_{B})}_{\ell}(q),h^{(N_{B})}_{\ell^{\prime}}(q)\right].

The dense reference map is denoted by S0​(ℓ,ℓ′)S_{0}(\ell,\ell^{\prime}), corresponding to NB=0N_{B}=0.

We quantify geometry drift relative to the dense reference by

Δ​SNB​(ℓ,ℓ′)=|SNB​(ℓ,ℓ′)−S0​(ℓ,ℓ′)|.\Delta S_{N_{B}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime})=\left|S_{N_{B}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime})-S_{0}(\ell,\ell^{\prime})\right|. (5)

Larger values of Δ​SNB​(ℓ,ℓ′)\Delta S_{N_{B}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime}) indicate a larger departure of that layer pair from the dense-model geometry.

In Fig. 4a, we visualize an all-end-layer drift profile

Δ​S¯NB​(ℓ)=⟨Δ​SNB​(ℓ,ℓ′)⟩ℓ′>ℓ,\overline{\Delta S}_{N_{B}}(\ell)=\left\langle\Delta S_{N_{B}}(\ell,\ell^{\prime})\right\rangle_{\ell^{\prime}>\ell},

where the average is taken over all valid end layers for each start layer ℓ\ell. In Fig. 4b, we further report two scalar summaries: an output-side average over a fixed set of layer pairs near the output end, and a global average over all valid layer pairs.

Data availability

The benchmark data used for the main evaluation are publicly available from their original providers or through the task interfaces of the Language Model Evaluation Harness. The post-compression recovery data were constructed from public or openly accessible instruction-tuning, mathematical-reasoning, code, summarisation and web-education sources for LLaMA2-7B and Qwen3-8B, together with generated arithmetic examples where specified. Dataset-construction details needed to reproduce the reported experiments are available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request.

Code availability

The MixT implementation and scripts for structural replacement, weight-matching initialisation, post-compression recovery, evaluation and resource profiling are being prepared for public release. During peer review, code required to reproduce the main results is available from the corresponding authors upon reasonable request.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
